svg.text: DevSecOps — where each control actually sits
stops a secret ever entering git history
stops a vulnerable image reaching the registry
limits what a compromise can do
A secret caught by a pre-commit hook costs thirty seconds. The same secret caught after it reaches
a public repository costs a credential rotation, an incident review and a very bad afternoon.
Every control above is cheaper the further left it sits. That is the entire idea behind shift left.
None of these replaces the others
A scanner does not make an image safe. It tells you what is known today about what you already built.
Runtime hardening does not stop a vulnerable dependency being shipped.
A review does not catch a CVE published next Tuesday against a base image you shipped last month.
They are layers. Each one assumes the others will sometimes fail.
